OBITUARY REFERENCE 
THE DEPUTY CHAIRMAN: Hon. Members, I refer with profound 
orrow to the passing awary of Shri R.M. Desai, a former Member of this ouse 
on the 26th July, 2002, at the age of 81. 
Born at village Vadahalli, district Bijapur in Karnataka, Shri Desai .ad 
his education at YadahalH, Bijapur, Dharwad and Belgaum. an agriculturist 
by vocation, Shri Desai served as the Commandant, Home Guards, in Taluka 
Bilji, from 1947 to 1956. He also served as the Chairman of the Karnataka State 
Road Transport Corporation from April 1976 to April 1982. He was also 
associated with various welfare organisations. 
Shri R.M. Desai started his legislative career as a Member of the Mysore 
Legislative Assembly in 1957, and remained its Member till 1969. He represented 
the State of Karnataka in this House from April, 1976 to April, 1982. 
We deeply mourn the passing away of Shri R.M. Desai. 
I request Members to rise in their places and observe silence as a mark of 
respect to the memory of the departed. 
(Horn. Members then stood in silence for one minute.) 
THE DEPUTY CHAIRMAN: Secretary-General will convey to the 
members of the bereaved family our sense of profound sorrow and deep 
sympathy.

ORAL ANSWERSTO QUESTIONS 
Question No. 221 
[The questioner (Shri Sukhdev Singh Libra) was absent. For answer vide 
pages 26 infra.] 
THE DEPUTY-CHAIRMAN: Question No. 222. 
SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA: Madam, Question Nos. 222 and 224 can 
be clubbed. 
SHRI PRANAB MUKHERJEE: That deals with smuggling of narcotic 
substances. 
THE DEPUTY CHAIRMAN: Yes, we can do that. But, Mr. Rama 
Muni Reddy should be there to put his question. Is he there? No, he is not there. 
Okay, we will take up only Question No. 222. 
Utilisation of seized narcotics 
*222. SHRI K. KALAVENKATA RAO: Will the Minister of FINANCE 
AND COMPANY AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Narcotics Control Bureau (NCB) lights up narcotics seized by it; 
and 
(b) if so, the reasons for not utilizing some of them like Ganja for 
manufacturing medicinal drugs under Government supervision? 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI 
JASWANT SINGH): (a) Yes, Sir. Seized narcotic drugs, other than opium, 
morphine, code in and thebaine, are destroyed. 
(b) Seized opium, morphine, codein and thebaine are utilized for 
extraction of alkaloids for medicinal and scientific use. Ganja does not have 
any utility for manufacturing medicinal drugs. 
SHRI K. KALAVENKATA RAO: Madam, my first supplementary is 
this. On June 26, 2002, about 450 kgs. Of seized drugs, worth Rs. 10 crores 
were lit by the Delhi Unit of the Narcotic Control Bureau. The burning 
caused a lot of pollution. I would like to know whether the Government 
would consider some alternative measures to utilise the seized Ganja and 
Heroin which are also used for medicinal purposes as 
2 
 

[30 July, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
pain-killers, etc. Cannot we utilise them for drug manufacturing under 
Government agencies? 
SHRI JASWANT SINGH: Madam, it is not medically established that 
Ganja or any derivative from Ganja can be utilised. Therefore, successive 
Government have felt that it is best destroyed. It cannot be put to medicinal 
use. Nor can any medicinal derivative be obtained from it. 
SHRI K. KALAVENKATA RAO: Do the government ensure that some part 
of the seized drugs do not reach the illicit trafficking market for drug abuse? 
SHRI JASWANT SINGH: Madam, I do not know if have got the 
question quite right. But it relates to drug abuse. So far as India is concerned, 
the factor of drug abuse has a very different connotation, as it has to, from 
particularly the developed western world. In our case, most of the addiction is 
limited to Opium or Ganja or Hashish. Over the years, ?cially, there is only 
limited acceptability in other than urban centres, of psychotropic drugs or 
derivatives of Opium, etc. But there is the addiction of problem. But the State 
and the society deal with it. There are very severe and stringent laws in this 
regard that have been introduced. For example, the NDPS Act is a very 
stringent Act whereby even the possession of a small quantity of Opium or 
such a drug invites a very severe penalty, these are legislative measures that are 
taken to discourage the tendency. The society also plays a role, perhaps a 
stronger one, in this. 
SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA: Madam, I would like to know from the 
hon. Minister how much quantity we realy need of this Opium, Morphine, Codein and 
Thebaine for our medical purposes. And how do you meet that demand? Do we 
meet that demand from seizures or do we produce these substances, or, do we 
have much more substance due to smuggling? What kind of planning is there? 
If we have still much more quantity of these substances, what do we do with 
those substances? Dou you destroy them or do you export them, because there is a 
complete confusion about the handling of these items? 
SHRI JASWANT SINGH: Sir, it is a fair question, but, an unfair 
observation that there is a complete confusion. There is, in fact, not complete 
confusion. India is amongst the few countries in the world, where 
3 

RAJYA SABHA [30 July, 2002] 
opium production is illicit. It is true that the Government controls these 
substances, and through the Government, pattas are granted. There are three 
States of the Union, where opium is cultivated, that is, Rajasthan, Madhya 
Pradesh and parts of Uttar Pradesh. The total production of opium, on an average, 
depending on yield etc., Mannually, is about 1,000 tonnes. But, it varies, and the 
figure that I have given of 1,000 tonnes, can of course, not be a figure that obtains 
every year, because, this is a fluctuating thing. On an average, India exports about 
400 tonnes to 500 tonnes of opium; export it to Europe, and to the United States 
of America principally for pharmaceutical uses. There is a certain limited 
requirement in India for pharmaceutical uses. We have, therefore, every year, a 
carry forward stock of a certain amount of residual opium. I am not giving you 
the exact figure, though if you are interested, I can always sent th£ exact last ounce 
account to you, as is available. We have roughly about t,700 tonnes of stored 
opium. We have two factories, where opium is purified. One is in Madhya 
Pradesh at Neemuch, and the other is in Uttar Pradesh at Gazi. We have only 
recently started a project — started in the sense — that H have required the 
Department to immediately commission a study. These are very old factories 
which were established during the British days, and have really run out of their 
purpose, other than really collecting opium, purifying it, storing it, weighing it, 
etc. So, how to modernise these factories so that the opium can be used by us for 
production of alkaloids or for such other pharamceutial requirements? The project 
report will be prepared for that, and I am sure, we will be able to meet the cost of 
setting up of these factories internally, from within the Finance Ministry, it 
necesary, with joint participation with one our pharamaceutical companies in 
India. 
SHRI C.P. THIRUNAVUKKARASU: Madam, the police and the 
various authorities constituted under the Act, are seizing opium, morphine, code in, 
thebaine, and other substances, and they have been destroying the same by 
setting them on fire. After seizure, these substances are sent to court to prove 
the case. I would like to know whether-after sending these substances to the court 
for the disposal of the cases-the authorities get back those materials from the 
custody of the court, and use those substances for the preparation of 
medicines or not. 
SHRI JASWANT SINGH: Madam, I must disabuse the mind of the hon. 
Member of the notion that the court keeps the seized drugs. The court has no 
use for the seized drugs like heroin. In the Court it is produced 
4

only as evidence. It is not only the police which is only a part of it. There is the 
Narcotics Control Bureau of the Government, and we also have a full-fledged 
administration in this regard. Do these drugs come back? Of course, they come 
back to the Finance Ministry, to the Narcotics Control Bureau, and others, and 
they have been utilised in a manner that is required or are set on fire to end this 
problem.

Norms for Maximum Permissible Bank Finance 
*221. SHRI SUKHDEV SINGH LIBRA: Will the Minister of FINANCE 
AND COMPANY AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Reserve Bank of India has laid certain norms for fixing 
the MPBF for the corporate customers taking into consideration the receivables 
of associate group of companies like investment made by the holding 
companies in the associate group of companies; and 
27 

RAJYA SABHA [30 July, 2002] 
(b) if so, what are the guidelines given to public sector banks for 
assessment of working captial finance of corporate customers/existing 
borrowers? 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI 
JASWANT SINGH): (a) and (b) Reserve Ba nk of India (RBI) had, in 1975, 
prescribed norms for fixing Maximum Permissible Bank Finance (MPBF), based 
on the recommendations of a Study Group headed by the then Chairman of 
Punjab National Bank. Over the year s, various improvements have been 
introduced in the loan delivery system. In April, 1997, norms for assessment of 
working capital needs, based on the concept of MPBF, were withdrawn by RBI. 
Banks are now free to evolve, with the approval of their Board of Directors, 
methods for assessing the working capital requirements according to their own 
perception of the borrower, also the credit needed by the borrower, Banks have 
been advised to lay down transparent policy and guidelines for credit 
dispensation in respect of each broad category of economic activity. Banks, do 
however, continue to be governed by the exposure norms relating to single/group 
borrower(s) and pudential norms prescribed by RBI.

Aircraft employee ratio in IA 
*226. SHRI PREM CHAND GUPTA: Will the Minister of CIVIL 
AVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Indian Airlines plans to shed 7,000 
personnel as a cost saving measure to bring its aircraft employee ratio down 
to international standards; 
(b) whether the ratio will still be double of what it is in Singapore 
Airlines where the ratio is as low as 161 per aircraft: and 
(c) if so, in what manner the airlines plans to achieve this and what is 
the time-frame for its completion? 
THE MINISTER OF CIVIL AVIATION (SHRI SYED 
SHAHNAWAZ HUSSAIN): (a) to (c) the staff strength of India Airlines 
including Alliance Air (a wholly owned subsidiary of Indian Airlines) as on 
31 st May, 2002 is 20,605. with the current strength of 57 aircraft, the 
aircraft/employee ratio is 1:361. This ratio is normally not comparable with 
other international airlines as the requirement of the employees varies from 
airlines to airline, and it also depends on extent of operation, nature of fleet 
and activities undertaken directly; 
There is present no proposal to shed 7000 personnel to bring down the 
aircraft/employee ratio. Indian Airlines has, however, taken various steps to 
contain its manpower by freezing fresh recruitment in non-operational 
categories and rolling back retirement age from 60 to 58 years and is also 
considering introducing a Voluntary Retirement Scheme.

THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI 
RAM NAIK): (a) to (d) To discuss various issues, inter-ministerial 
consultations were done by Ministry of Road Transport and Highways 
(MORTH). Different aspects including problems relating to the existing 
retail outlets on the highways as well as the future retail outlets, that may be

(ii) Pre-1983 fuel stations to be identified along with their deficiencies

deceleration and acceleration lanes would be provided by the oil 
companies.

National Highway to the fuel station and the licence fee for the 
existing fuel station shall be as per the existing norms. 
(v) Fuel stations falling within the municipal limits to follow the 
municipal rules, petroleum rules and MORTH's norms. 
For future retail outlets, norms are yet to be finalized.

*233.   SHRIMATI AMBIKA SONI: 
DR.T. SUBBARAMI REDDY: 
Will the Minister of FINANCE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether RBI has decided to monitor banks' participation in farm 
lending; 
(b) whether this move is aimed at increasing commercial banks' 
increased participation in overall agri-lending; 
(c) if so, the details of commercial banks which have agreed to 
participate in farm lending; 
40 
 

[30 July, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
(d) whether this will give a great boost to the agriculture sector in the 
country; and

out by the RBI?

(SHRIJASWANT SINGH): (a) to (d) Yes, Sir. Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has 
been regularly monitoring the progress made by banks in their lending to 
agriculture. To increase the flow of lending through commercial banks as also 
for their increased participation RBI has issued extant guidelines according to 
which all domestic scheduled commercial banks are required to land 40% of their 
Net Bank Credit (NBC) to priority sector, of which 18% is stipulated for 
agriculture sector.This measure is aimed at boosting the agriculture sector in the 
country. 
(e) RBI has formulated a time-frame of two years within which both 
public and private sector banks should achieve this target of 18% for landing 
to agriculture. Accordingly, banks have beeifcadvised to take necessary steps 
so as to reach this target by March, 2003. In addition, RBI has also taken the 
following steps for increasing the flow of credit to agriculture sector: 
• Formulating of Special Agricultural Credit Plans by public sector banks 
with a view to achieve distinct and marked improvement; 
• Opening of atleast one specialized agricultural finance branch by all 
scheduled commercial banks in each State; 
• Introduction has issue of Kisan Credit Cards for farmers; 
• Setting up of rural Infrastructure Development Fund (RIDF) to assist State 
Government in quick completion of rural infrastructural projects; 
• Introduction of a scheme for financing agri-clinics and agri-business centres 
to accelerate the process of technology transfer to agriculture and providing 
supplementary sources of input supply and services; 
• Introduction of a scheme for financing small and marginal farmers for 
purchase of land for agricultural purposes; 
• Increasing the limit for financing of distribution of inputs for allied 
activities to Rs. 25 lakhs; and 
• Increasing the credit limit for produce (marketing) loan to Rs. 5 lakh.

the menace. This issue was also di scussed at the 45 Session of the

enforcement agencies to keep a close watch on such activities with a view to

Problems faced by coffee growers in Kamataka 
*236. SHRI K.B. KRISHNA MURTHY: Will the Minister of COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that the coffee planters in 
Kamataka are faced with the problem of declining coffee exports due to crash 
in prices globally; 
(b) whether the recent notification of Central Board of Direct Taxes 
subjecting 25 per cent of the realization from the sale of coffee to central Income 
Tax has crippled them further; and 
(c) whether Government would provide an exit option to the coffee 
growers in Kamataka, 98 per cent of whom are small farmers to opt for 
Agricultural Tax (AIT) which is more rational and quantitative? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY (SHRI RAJIV PRATAP RUDI): (a) Yes Sir. Coffee is 
globally traded and export oriented commodity and its prices are decided at New 
York Exchange and'London Exchange for Arabica and Robusta respectively. In 
recent times the global coffee production has outstripped consumption leading to 
mismatch between demand and supply resulting in steep fall in international 
coffee prices. The price fall has affected all 
52 

[30 July, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
coffee producing countries including India, since 80% of coffee produced in 
the country is exported, the industry is mainly dependent on the global coffee 
prices. Due to low coffee prices prevailing in the international markets, there 
has been a slight decline in the export of coffee during 2001 -02 as compared 
to the previous year. 
(b) As the notification has been issued very recently, it is too early to 
assess the actual impact of the same on the small coffee growers. 
(c) Does not arise in view of (b) above.

WTO Assistance for Trade Negotiation 
1376. SHRI R.P. GOENKA: Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is fact that India has sought assistance from the World Trade 
Oprganisation in some specific areas of research, training and institution — 
building, under the $ 30 million Technical Assistance and Capacity Building 
Fund, set -up recently to assist developing and less developed countries in the 
trade negotiation process; and 
(b) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY (SHRI RAJIV PRATAP RUDI): (a) and (b) At the Fourth 
Ministerial Conference of the WTO held at Doha, the members confirmed that 
technical cooperation and capacity building are core elements of the 
development dimension of the multilateral trading system. It was decided to 
develop a plan to ensure long term, secure and predictable funding for the 
WTO technical assistance activities. Pursuant to the mandate contained in the 
Doha Ministerial Declaration, the General Council decided to convene a 
Pledging Conference and also to create the Doha Development Agenda 
Global Trust Fund. In the Pledging Conference held on 11th March, 2002, the 
member governments pledged to the Global Trust Fund an amount of over 30 
million Swiss Francs for the WTO to conduct the technical assistance and 
capacity building activities for the developing countries for their constructive 
and fruitful participation in the Doha Work Programme. 
The Coordinated WTO Secretariat Annual Technical Assistance Plan 2002, 
which is being implemented lists various technical assistance activities for the 
developing countries including LDCs. 
For India, the activities listed included Technical Missions on Trade and 
Competition Policy, Trade and Investment (in cooperation with the 
UNCTAD), Trade Facilitation, Integrated Data Base, Services, Intensive 
Training Course for Asia and Pacific Region to be organised in New Delhi (in 
cooperation with the UNCTAD) and a Regional Workshop on SPS 
Agreement. Further action in respect of these activities and others considered 
necessary will be taken in accordance with our felt needs at the appropriate 
time.

(c) the action proposed to be taken to boost export of India Coffee? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY (SHRI RAJIV PRATAP RUDI): (a) and (b) Due to low 
prices of coffee prevailing in the international market and also increase in the 
domestic consumption of coffee from 60,000 MT to 70,000 MT, there has been a 
decline in coffee exports from India during 2001-2002 as compared to the 
previous years. 
90 

[30 July, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) To boost Indian coffee exports as well as to maximise export 
earnings, the Coffee Board is implementing a medium term export strategy during 
the current plan period.The key initiatives identified in the strategy to improve 
coffee exports from India are as under:— 
— Shifting product mix in favor of Arabica. 
— Cost reduction to improve competitiveness. 
— Improving quality perception of Indian coffee. 
— Integrating Indian coffee with the global coffee trade. 
— Guarantee reliability of exporters. 
— Carryout a major communication initiative in key overseas markets to 
enhance the image of Indian coffee as well as to improve market 
share. 
— Participation in important overseas trade fairs involving exporters and 
grower exporters. 
— Organising buyer-seller meets between Indian exporters and 
overseas buyers in key markets. 
— Hosting visits of roaster/buyer delegation from leading consuming 
countries to Indian coffee tracks and facilitating interaction with the 
industry representatives. 
— Organising "cupping" of Indian coffees by international coffee 
experts to evaluate and propagate the finer attributes of Indian 
coffees. 
— Institution of Export awards to encourage exporters. 
Competitiveness of industrial groups 
†1384. SHRIMATI SAVITA SHARDA: Will the Minister of 
COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government are considering to take steps to 
make industrial groups more competitive at the international level; 
(b) if so, whether Government have taken any steps in this regard;  
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
91 

RAJYA SABHA [30 July, 2002] 
(c) if so, the details thereof; and 
(d) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY (DR. RAMAN SINGH): (a) to (d) The Government's 
approach to industrial sector growth and development is that of increasing 
efficiency and competitiveness of the Indian industry to enable them to stand 
on their own in the face of global competition. This approach is manifested in 
the broad strategy enunciated in the Union Budget 2002-2003, which lays 
emphasis on deepening structural reforms and regeneration of industrial sector. 
In pursuance of this approach and strategy, Government has initiated several 
measures which are mentioned below:— 
• The Union Budget 2002-2003 has made allocations towards some of the 
major schemes, which will strengthen infrastructure and boost 
demand especially in construction housing steel and cement sectors. 
These schemes include PM's Gram Sadak Yojana, Infrastructure 
Equity Fund, Urban Reform Incentive Fund, City Challenge Fund, 
are Accelerated Power Development Reform Programme. 
• DIPP has entrusted sector-wise studies in respect of capital goods, pulp and 
paper and cement industries to organisations of international repute 
with a view to assess global competitiveness of these industries. 
• The Administrative Price Mechanism (APM) in the petroleum sector 
has been dismantled w.e.f. 1.04.2002. The market forces will now 
determine the prices in the petroleum sector. 
• To deal with the forces of competition, industrial and other 
companies require restructuring on a continuous basis. For this 
purpose it is essential to promote ou t of court mechanisms for timely 
and transparent corporate debt restructuring of viable debt entities. A 
mechanism for Corporate Debt Restructuring (CDR) has been set up 
under the guidelines issued by the RBI. 
• To improve the operating environment of the companies and to 
improve business confidence, the Companies Act has been amended 
to allow buyback of shares, by the companies. 
• To deepen reforms in stock exchanges and to provide protection 
92 

[30 July, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
to the investors, Union Budget 2002-2003 proposes amendments inSEBI 
Act 1992. 
• The draft Electricity Bill has been introduced in the Parliament for 
facilitating comprehensive power sector reforms. 
• The Competition Bill has been introduced in the Parliament for 
promoting competition and curbing monopoly. 
• The RBI has cut Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) to 5 per cent from 5.5 
per cent a move that is likely to release Rs. 5000 crores to banks for 
lending.This move will ease the liquidity position further. 
• The Reserve Bank has also announced measures for stepping up 
growth momentum with stimulus to agriculture, housing, small-scale 
sector and exports in its credit policy for 2002-03. It also aims at 
facilitating better credit delivery and moving forward with structural 
reforms. 
• Power sector reforms have received a boost in pursuance of the centre's 
decision to provide grants equal to the amount by which States have 
been able to reduce their power sector deficits. The States of Haryana, 
Rajasthan and Andhra Pradesh have been able to reduce losses in the 
past couple of years. These three States will now be eligible for 
matching grant under the Accelerated Power Development and Reform 
Programme (APDRP).

  SHRIMATIVANGA GEETHA:

SHRIMATI SAVITA SHARDA:  
SHRI RUMANDLA RAMACHANDRAIAH:       
Will the Minister of FINANCE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether the Government's attention has been drawn to the news-item 
captioned "VRS Income exempted from Tax" which appeared in "Deccan 
Chronicle (English) on 21 st June, 2002; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether the employees who retired from the bank service under VRS 
on 31 March 2001 and payment made during April-December, 2001 are also 
exempted from tax; 
.(d) if so, the details thereof, if not, the reasons therefor; 
(e) whether the Ministry of Finance propose to give tax exemption to such 
bank employees from VRS income; and 
(f) whether any modifications amending rules are likely to be issued by 
Government? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE AND 
COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI GINGEE N. RAMACHANDRAN): (a) and (b) 
Yes, Sir. 
Through Notification No. 151/2002 dated 19-06-2002, Rule 2BA of 
Income-tax Rules has been amended to provide that amount received by an 
employee of a notified institution having importance throughout India or in any 
State or States, at the time of his voluntary retirement shall be exempt if the 
scheme of voluntary retirements is framed in accordance with the conditions 
prescribed in the said Rule 2BA. These conditions, inter alia, stipulated that the 
employees must have completed 10 years of service or 40 years of age, etc. the 
exemption, however, would be available only to the extent of Rs. 5 lakhs as 
provided in section 10(10C) of the Income-tax Act. The whole of VRS income 
received by the employees would, therefore, be not exempt from tax.

Transparency in Transactions of Governments Securities 
1409. SHRI NILOTPAL BASU: Will the Minister of FINANCE AND 
COMPANY AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that trading in Government Securities are not 
allowed in stock Exchanges across the counter in a transparent manner on 
screen and in a demutualised form; 
(b) if so, the present practice of trade in G-secs and details arising 
thereof; 
(c) whether the present practice does not have inbuilt safeguards against 
fraud as revealed in the Home Trade case; 
(d) if so, whether any changes are being contemplated in the present practice 
and introuduce trade under across the counter transactions in the exchanges; 
and 
(e) if so, the details thereof and the tentative schedule in this 
regard? 
121 

RAJYA SABHA [30 July, 2002] 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE AND 
COMPANY AFFARIS (SHRI ANANT GANGARAM GEETE): (a) and (b) 
Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has intimated that transactions in Government 
securities can take place in the following ways: 
1. Over The Counter (OTC) market: Deals are contracted either directly 
between participants or through the medium of a broker. RBI regulated 
entities such as banks, primary dealers, financial institutions, etc. can 
only use the services of brokers registered with the NSE, BSE or 
OTCEI. 
2. Negotiated Dealing System (NDS): With effect from February 15, 2002, 
NDS has been operationalised. NDS is a screen based system set-up 
by RBI that not only ensures transparency but also enables settlement 
in RBI either directly beyond a limit or through Clearing Corporation 
of India Limited. (CCIL). 
3. Stock Exchanges : The exchanges provide both screen based order 
given trading (i.e., continuous) or negotiated market in Government 
securities. 
(c) The transactions unertaken by certain cooperative banks dealing 
with Home Trade show that the concerned cooperative banks had violated 
the RBI regulations and guidelines. Where the settlement is directly in the 
books of the RBI, the Delivery Versus Payment (DVP) system ensures 
that transfer of funds does not take place unless there is delivery of 
securities and wee versa. 
The Home Trade transactions purportedly relate to buying of 
Government securities in physical form. In the absence of any delivery of 
transfer of securities for month together, such transactions tantamount to making 
a clean advance in the guise of securities transactions. 
(d) and (e) In the light of recent fraudulent transactions in the guise 
of Government securities transactions in physical format by a few co 
operative banks with the help of some broker entities, RBI proposd to 
accelerate the measures under contemplation for further reducing the 
scope for trading in physical form., RBI, thus issued a circular on 
"Transactions in Government securities" on 20th May, 2002, taking the 
following measures to expedite convers ion if all Government securities 
into demat modes: 
(i) All RBI regulated entities [including Financial Institutions (FIs), 
122 

[30 July, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
Primary Dealers (PDs), cooperative banks, RRBs, Local Area Banks 
(LABs), Non Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs)] were advised to 
undertake purchase/sales transactions with efect from July 1, 2002 
compulsorily through Subsidiary General Ledger (SGL)/Constituent 
Subsidiary General Ledger (CSGL)/demat accounts. 
(ii) All RBI regulated entities were advised to mandatorily hold their 
investments in Government securities in SGL/CSGL account or in a 
demat account with depositories. 
(iii) All RBI regulated entities were prohibited from undertaking any 
transactions in physical form with any broker.

† 1443. SHRIMATI SAVITA SHARDA: Will the Minister of FINANCE 
AND COMPANY AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that issuing of fake letter of credits is going on a 
large scale in the counry;

(d) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE AND 
COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI ANANT GANGARAM GEETE): (a) to (d) 
Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has intimated that on the basis of frauds reported 
by the banks to RBI, it cannot be stated that issue of fake Letter of Credits (LCs) 
is going on at a mass level in the country. 
RBI has advised banks from time to time the common fraud prone areas 
and the measures required to be taken for their prevention. Some of the specific 
safeguards required to be taken by banks for prevention of LC related frauds are 
that LCs-should not normally be opened for customers who do not enjoy the credit 
facilities with the bank and if any such request is received the bank should 
subject the proposal to thorough scrutiny including reference to the bank in 
which the importer enjoys the credit facilities, reasons for approaching bank 
for opening of LCs and the genuineness of the customer. Bank should ensure 
that the importer has a valid import licence. Before establishing the LC the 
bank should satisfy itself that the customer is in a position to retire the bills 
drawn under LC and prescribe suitable margin and other security as 
necessary/LC above Rs. 10,000/- should be signed by two officials with a view 
to minimize the malpractices by the bank officials and blank LC forms should 
be treated as security items. Adequate safeguards against their pilferage should 
be taken. -[Original notice of the question was received in Hindi.

Global Meet of Parliamentarians and on AIDs/HIV 
*203. SHRI AIMADUDDIN AHMED KHAN (DURRU): Will the Minister 
of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Parliamentarians from across the global met in Delhi in May 
this year to pledge concrete steps to address the challenges of AIDS/HIV 
epidemic, effectively; 
(b) whether around 15,000 people are afflicted by the deadly disease 
everyday; 
(c) if not, the estimated number of persons afflicted day after day in India; 
and 
(d) the details of the declaration adopted in the global meet and the steps 
taken and being taken by Government in the light of the declaration? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI 
SHATRUGHAN SINHA): (a) to (d)The International Policy makers Conference 
on HIV/AIDS was held in New Delhi on May 11th-12fth, 2002. Convened by 
Member of Parliament, Shri Kapil Sibal, this Conference was organized by 
the National AIDS Control Organization, the Indian Council of Medical 
Research and the International AIDS Vaccine. Initiative as part of a Memorandum 
of Understanding signed by these, organizations. 
204 

[30 July, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
The Conference was convened to discuss and deliberate an action plan that 
address an entire range of issues rela ting to HIV and AIDS. Prime Minister, 
Shri Atal Bihari Vajpayee inaugurated this International Policy Makers 
Conference, Prominently attended by the Leader of the Opposition, Shrimati 
Sonia Gandhi, by Chief Minister of Andhra Pradesh, Maharashtra and Karnataka 
as well as by Ministers representing both the central and the state governments. 
Parliamentarians from eight countries namely South Africa, Kenya, Uganda, 
Nigeria, Thailand, Nepal, China and Brazil participated in the conference. 
Additionally, delegates and resource persons from several national and 
international organizations, NGOs and donor agencies participated. . 
2. UNAIDS and WHO have estimated that by the end of 2001, 40 
million adults and children were living with HIV/AIDS around the world. 
During the year 2001 alone, an estimated 5 million people are estimated to have 
become infected. Each day of the year, about 15,000 people are estimated to be 
getting infected by this deadly virus. 
3. In India, the estimates for HIV infections during 1998, 1999 and 2000 
and 2001 have been 3.5 million, 3.7 million, 3.86 million 3.97 million 
respectively. 
4. The presence of high-level political persons cutting across party lines 
at the International Policy Makers Conference demonstrated unambiguously, 
a strong political commitment within India at the highest level, cutting across 
party lines, to address HIV/AIDS in a meaningful manner. Resultantly, the 
Delhi Declaration given in the statement was adopted at the conclusion of the 
Conference {See below). 
5. The main features of the Delhi declaration are: (i) to inform, educate, 
communicate and develop strategies, working closely with affected countries 
to promote effective AIDS prevention initiatives; (ii) to identify and begin to 
address those factors that make individuals particularly vulnerable to HIV 
infection, including underdevelopment, poverty, illiteracy, (iii) to promote 
social acceptance and respect for the dignity and rights of all people affected 
by HIV/AIDS and to oppose all forms of stigma and discrimination; (iv) to 
make every effort to provide progressively and in a sustainable manner, the 
highest attainable standard of treatment and care to people living with HIV/AIDS; 
(v) to support research and development of AIDS vaccines and other prevention 
technologies, 
205 

RAJYA SABHA [30 July, 2002] 
keeping in mind the pressing needs of the developing world; (vi) to create an 
enabling environment and build capacity among policy-maker in respective 
countries, and in particular, seek to strengthen legislation and regulatory systems 
and procedure; (vii) to mobilise political commitment at national, regional and 
global levels; and (viii) to promote collaborative efforts among governments, 
peoples representatives, private industry, international agencies and non-
governmental organisations to move forward the commitments made in this 
Declaration. 
Following the Conference, several initiatives are in hand: 
1. A Working Group has been constituted to carry forward the 
recommendations emerging out of the Delhi Declaration and the 
conference. Both the National AIDS Control Organisation and the Indian 
Council of Medical Research representing government, are a part of this 
Working Group. The other members include members of the positive 
people's network, NGOs international agencies and the media.This Working 
Group will examine ways to address the recommendations that emerged 
from the four themes of the Conference, namely: 
(i) Knowledge and behaviour change 
(ii) The adoption of new technologies 
(iii) Care and Treatment 
(iv) Global resources 
2. A sub-group has been formed to look at a comprehensive legislation 
on HIV/AIDS for India, that will typically address issues of stigma and 
discrimination, confidentiality in testing and counseling, trials for new 
treatment, and access to care, treatment, travel, insurance and employment. 
Members of this Sub-group include NGOs, a member of the positive person's 
network, the Indian Council of Medical Research and the National AIDS 
Control organisation. 
3. A website is on the anvil that will promote and facilitate interaction 
between national and international parliamentarians who participated in the 
Conference. Efforts are on to reach out to all parliamentarians within India, and 
also to a global network who are concerned about issues related to HIV/AIDS. 
206 

[30 July, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
4. Govt, will also facilitate a Parliamentary forum, which would seek to 
both mobilise and sustain political support for at the national level and at State 
levels. 
Government has already initiated some action listed in the Delhi 
Declaration, such as: 
(i) People living with HIV/AIDS (PLHAs) are being actively involved in 
policy-making forums like the National AIDS Committee, and also in 
the Executive Committee of the State AIDS Control Societies. They 
are encouraged to actively contribute towards design and 
implementation of project and programme in the Advisory 
committees. 
(ii) NACO has formulated guidelines for "Drop in Centre" to encourage 
information sharing and networking of PLHAs among themselves. It is 
anticipated that this will create an enabling environment for 
     dialogue and discussion with concerned stakeholders. 
(iii) Government has initiated sensitisation programmes of panchayat raj 
institutions and these are expected to eliminate stigma and 
discrimination against PLHAs. 
(iv) In order to prevent the spread of HIV/AIDS amongst vulnerable and 
marginalised population groups like Commercial Sex Workers (CSWS), 
Truck Drivers, Migrant Workers, Men having Sex with Men (MSM), 
Street Children, injecting Drug Users (IDUs), Jail Inmates, etc. 680 
intervention projects are being implemented by NGOs that attempt to 
bring about behaviour change through peer education and the promotion 
of condom usage as well as treatment for sexually transmitted infections 
etc. 
(v) Drugs for the treatment of opportunistic infections have been made 
available in public sector hospitals in the country for the 
management of HIV/AIDS patient s. Besides, community care & 
support is being encouraged by establishing Community Care Centres 
through NGOs in different parts of the country. At present there are 36 
such centres functioning in the country. 
(vi) In order to address issues of access and equality in respect of 
treatment, Government is continually striving to bring about 
reductions in the high cost of anti-retro-viral drugs so that they 
become more affordable. Government has now exempted these drugs 
from custom & excise duties.

Statement 
Delhi Declaration 
PARLIAMENTARIANS' COMMITMENT TOWARDS A WORLD WITHOUT AIDS 
May 11-12, 2002 
The HIV/AIDS epidemic constitutes a global health emergency of 
unprecedented magnitude that impacts economic and soial development world-
wide and in particular the developing world, to combat this global tragedy, a 
comprehensive strategy is needed to focus on issues including health-care, 
prevention, support, and treatment, within a legal framework designed to protect 
human rights. With 15,000 new HIV infections daily, there is no time to delay. 
We, the undersigned, pledge to provide leadership and take concrete 
action to address the complexities and challenges presented by the 
epidemic, building on the UN Declaration of Commitment on 
HIV/AIDS and other international, regional, and national 
agreement.† 
We pledge to actively involve affected communities, including 
organisations of people living with HIV/AIDS in policy formulation, and 
implementation. 
† Resolution S-26/2 adopted by the United Nations General Assembly on June 
27, 2001. 
208 

[30 July, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
We pledge to inform, educate, communicate and develop strategies, 
working closely with affected communities, to promote effective AIDS 
prevention initiatives. 
We pledge to identify and begin to address those factors that make 
individuals particularly vulnerable to HIV infection, including 
underdevelopment, poverty, illiteracy, lack of empowerment of women, and all 
types of sexual exploitation. 
We pledge to promote social acceptance and respect for the dignity and 
rights of all people affected by HIV/AIDS and to oppose all forms of stigma 
and discrimination. 
We pledge to increase awareness and upgrade knowledge in societies inhabited 
by ignorance and deep seated cultural and social prejudices. 
We pledge to make every effort to provide progressively and in a 
sustainable manner, the highest attainable standard of treatment and care to people 
living with HIV/AIDS. 
We pledge to support research and development of AIDS vaccines and 
other prevention technologies, keeping in mind the pressing needs of the 
developing world. 
We pledge to support the acceleration of scientific progress, adhering to the 
highest ethical standards in the research, development, delivery, and use to 
prevention technologies. 
We pledge to work to build infrastructure and take other measures to 
ensure access to and effective use of affordable, life-saving AIDS treatment 
and future AIDS vaccines when they become available. 
We pledge to create an enabling environment and build capacity among 
policy-makers in our respective countries, and in particular, seek to strengthen 
legislation and regulatory systems and procedures. 
We pledge, as members of a global community, to strive for equitable 
distribution of essential resources needed to control the IDS epidemic and to 
enhance the quality of life of people living with HIV/AIDS. 
We pledge to mobilise political commitment with peoples' 
representatives to propel a comprehensive response at national, regional and 
global levels.

representatives, private industry, international agencies and nongovernmental 
organisations to move forward the commitments made in this Declaration. 
We pledge to put in place ongoing mechanisms for the implementation, 
monitoring and review of the Delhi Declaration.

Exorbitant charging by private blood banks 
† *206. SHRIMATI SAVITA SHARDA: Will the Minister of 
HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that private blood banks in the country are 
charging exorbitant price from patients; 
(b) if so. whether Government are considering to take any action to 
keep a check on such blood banks and prevent them from doing so; and 
(c) if so, the details thereof and by when, and if not, the reasons 
therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI 
SHATRUGHAN SINHA): (a) to (c) Selling of Whole Human Blood is 
prohibited and, therefore, no blood bank can charge any price for blood itserf. 
However, before the blood is issued by the blood-banks for-transfusion, it is 
mandatory under the provisions of Drugs and Cosmetics Rules to test each unit 
of blood collected for freedom from HIV 1 .& 2 antibodies, Hepatitis B 
Surface antigen, Hepatitis C antibody, Malaria and Syphilis. Some expenditure 
is incurred by the blood banks for conducting these mandatory test for 
transfusion transmitted diseases and for handling of blood. This expenditure 
has been estimated to be about Rs. 500/- and is recovered from the patients as 
service charges by the blood banks. 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
213 

RAJYA SABHA [30 July, 2002] 
2. Guideline have been issued by National AIDS Control Organisation 
(NACO) for recovery of service charges by blood banks in different sector. 
As per these guidlines, government and voluntary blood banks may charge 
Rs. 250/- per unit of blood as service charge for issuing blood to patients of 
their own hospitals or to other government or voluntary sector hospitals and 
subsidies rest of the cost. These blood banks while issueing blood to private 
nursing homes/hospitals may realise full processing cost of Rs. 500/-. The 
blood banks run in private sector may recover cost towards service charges to 
a maximum of Rs. 500/- per unit. The guidelines also permit cost recovery 
for additional tests (other than mandatory) done on the blood unit. 
3. It has been reported that by and large there is not much variation 
from NACO guidelines in the service charges being recovered by blood 
banks in the private sector in the country. However, it is noticed that some 
stand alone blood banks and blood banks attached to corporate or private 
sector recover service charges which are much higher than the one circulated 
by'lhe government on the grounds of carrying out test in addition to the 
mandatory tests and using consumables of higher price. 
4. Since different blood banks have varying overhead costs in handling 
and testing of blood, and since there is no legal provision to fix uniform blood 
processing charges, the blood banks are not being penalised for charging 
variable rates. However, the state bodies such as State AIDS Control 
Societies and State Blood Tranfusion councils are seized of this issue and 
from time to time during meeting with private blood banks, have been 
insisting and urging upon them to follow NACO guidelines on recovery of 
service charges.

1204. DR. ABRAR AHMED: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND

(b) There was a paradigm shift in the Family Welfare Programme after 
the International Conference on Population and Development (ICPD), Cairo in 
1994. The "Target Free Approach (TFA)" was adopted since 1st April, 1996 all

the year 2010. The major ones are— 
(1) to meet the demands in full for basic reproductive and child health 
services, supplies and infrastructure. 
(2) Reducing infant mortality rate to below 30 per 1000 live births. 
(3) Reducing maternal mortality to below 1000 per one lakh live births.

preventable diseases. 
(5) Achieving 80% institutional deliveries and 100% deliveries by 
trained persons.

child health services.

fertility by 2010. 
 
(10) Making school education up to age 14 free and compulsory and reduce

banks.

separate sterile syringes and needles for each injection.

cities/districts has been launched under National Immunization 
Programme.

immunized against Hepatitis-B. State Governments have also been 
advised to take similar steps.

Increase in polio cases 
† 1248. SHRI P.K. MAHESHWARI: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) the number of polio cases which came to light in the country during 
the last three years, State-wise; 
(b) whether it is a fact that cases of diseases like polio are increasing instead 
of decreasing despite pulse polio drive launched throughout the country; and 
(c) if so, the concrete steps Government are taking to prevent it? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) State-wise number of cases during

(b) and (c) The objective of the Government is eradicating Polio from the country 
and obtaining Polio-free certification by 2005. There has been significant progress 
towards achieving polio-free status. The number of Polio Cases has declined from 
1934 in 1998 to 1126 in 1999,265 in 2000, and 268 in 2001. Although the number of 
Polio cases in 2001 remained more or less the same as in 2000, the number of polio-
endemic districts in the courtry came down from 314 in 1998, to 192 in 1999, 89 in 
2000, and 63 in 2 001. Polio is endemic now mainly  in Uttar Pradesh and Bihar 
which accounted for 216 and 27 cases respectively in 2001 out of total 268. Mopup 
Vaccination rounds are being undertaken in high-risk districts of Uttar Pradesh and 
Bihar during low transmission seasons and in areas in which fresh cases of Polio are 
detected. The Government has planned two National Immunization Days, all over the 
country and two additional Sub National Immunizations Days in the States of U.P 
Bihar, Haryana and Delhi during the winter season of the current year.

Government propose to tackle the problem of diarrhoea during the peak 
period from May-August, 2002? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): The Government of India is 
implementing the National Surveillance Programme for Communicable 
Diseases (NSPCD) since 1997-98 in selected districts in the country.The 
objectives of the programme are generating early warning signals of 
outbreaks due to epidemic-prone communicable diseases including diarrhoea 
and other water-borne diseases and rapid response thereto,

promote the awareness among the people about this disease and the progress 
made in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) to (c) We have a system of annual 
sentinel surveillance being carried out every year since 1998. Prior to 1998, the 
estimated figures of HIV positive persons within India were 1.75 million. 
Subsequently, the estimated figures based on annual sentinel surveys are as 
follows:  
1998 3.5 million 
1999 3.7 million 
2000 3.86 million and 
2001 3.97 million 
However, it is noticed that the rate of increase of HIV infections within 
India is on the decline. 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
316 

[30 July, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
The Behavioural surveillance survey report 2001 shows that 46.8% of 
respondents were aware of the two important methods of prevention of 
transmission i.e. consistent condom use and sexual relationships with faithful 
and uninfected partners. 
3.4% of respondents stated that they suffered from genital discharge in the 
preceding 12 months. 
Proportion of respondents who reported genital discharge or ulcer/ sore or 
both within the reference period of past one year was 4.6%. 
The median age at first sex was 21 years for males and 18 years for females 
in the country. 
11.8% males and 2% females reported sex with non-regular partners in a 12-
month recall period. 
Out of these, 33.6% of males and 26.6% of females reported consistent 
use of condoms in sex with non-regular partners in a 12-month recall period. 
(d) The various activities undertaken to prevent and to promote the 
awareness among the people about this disease, are as follows: 
(i) An effective and sustained strategy to bring about changes in 
behaviour to prevent further spread of HIV infections has been adopted. A 
variety of communication tools for raising awareness and behvioural change 
are being carried out, which includes: 
Use of Mass Media 
Advocacy at various levels 
School AIDS Education Programme 
University Talk AIDS Programme 
Family Health Awareness Campaign 
Inter-Sectoral collaboration; etc. 
For prevention of spread of HIV infection among high risk groups like 
Commercial sex workers, Injecting drug users and truckers etc., targeted 
intervention projects are being implemented through NGOs.The services 
provided under these projects include peer counselling, condom 
317 

RAJYA SABHA [30 July, 2002] 
promotion, treatment of sexually transmitted infections and creation of 
enabling environment etc. 
(ii) Preventing intervention among general population is being carried out by 
providing voluntary testing and counselling services, safe blood transfusion 
services, early diagnosis and treatment of sexually transmitted infections and 
Promotion of condom use through free distribution and social marketing 
schemes. 
Financial assistance is provided to public sector hospitals for treatment 
of opportunistic infections. Support is also provided to NGOs for setting up 
community care centres to promote home based community care to such 
patients.

Revival scheme for National Instruments Ltd. 
1270. SHRI DIPANKAR MUKHERJEE: Will the Minister of HEAVY 
INDUSTRIES AND PUBLIC ENTERPRISES be pleased to state: 
(a) the status of the revival scheme sanctioned in 1999 by BIFR for 
National Instruments Ltd; 
(b) whether the scheme has been declared as "failed" and show cause 
notice of wining up issued by BIFR; 
(c) if so, the reasons therefor; 
(d) whether workers of the company are not getting salaries since 
December, 2001; 
(e) if so, the reasons therefor and the action to liquidate their dues; and 
(f) if not, the actual status of statutory dues, payable to the workers? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEAVY 
INDUSTRIES AND PUBIC ENTERPRISES (DR. VALLABHBHAI 
RAMJIBHAI KATHIRIA): (a) The Government has so far released Rs. 2.00 
crore for repair/renewals/replacement on the basis of the requirement 
projected by the Company. 
328 

[30 July, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
Further, Rs. 16.98 crore was released for VRS and the company has 
released 389 employees. Government counter guarantee for Rs. 4.55 crore 
has been provided to the Company. 
Capital Restructuring of the Company and conversion of loan into 
equity has been approved incumbent on Joint Venture (JV) formation for 
which action has been initiated 
The sanctioned scheme envisaged that the Company will mobilize Rs. 
13.47 crore from sale of 4 plots of land. So far, only one plot has been sold 
for Rs. 4.68 crore. The company is making vigorous efforts for sale of 
remaining 3 plots. 
(b) and (c) Yes, Sir. BIFR has issued a show cause notice on 13.6.2002 
that the company be wound up as the revival scheme has failed. 
The BIFR has observed that the performance of the Company has 
deteriorated resulting in increase of operating losses and the accumulated 
loss. Further, the Company/Government of india (GOI) has not been able to 
finalise the sale of the remaining 3 plots of surplus land. The GOI has also 
not provided the disired budgetary support of Rs. 5 crore for payment of 
salaries and wages. Also there is no likelihood of the networth of the 
company turning positive by 2002-03 as envisaged in the Revival and 
Modified Scheme Sanctiond by the Board. 
(d) to (f) Government has provided to the company a budgetary 
support of Rs. 184 lakhs in July, 2002 for payment to salaries/wages from 
August 2001 to Februray, 2002. In addition the Government has agreed to 
provide budgetary support of Rs. 6.79 crore for statutory and other dues.

Action to decongest Delhi 
1319. SHRI JANARDHANA POOJARY: Will the Minister of 
URBAN DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether Delhi is over-populated causing a heavy strain on power, 
water, sewage and roads and consequently causing heavy air pollution 
and health problems to the citizens; and 
(b) if so, the details in this regard and the action initiated by 
Government to decongest Delhi and the time-schedule drawn for achieving 
this objective? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (SHRI O. 
RAJAGOPAL): 
365 

RAJYA SABHA [30 July, 2002] 
(a) Yes. Sir. Statistically, as reported by DDA, Delhi is one of the fastest 
growing metropolis having a growth rate of 3.84% per annum.This increase in 
population puts strain on available infrastructure and services. 
(b) The Delhi Jal Board has reported that against required water of 800 
MGD, it has installed capacity of 631 MGD.Through optimization it is producing 
650 MGD.Thus, there is a shortfall of 150 MGD.Various short term and long 
term measures have been taken by DJB for augmentation of water supply. 
In regard to sewage, Delhi Jal Board has informed that all the urban 
villages, resettlement colonies and regularized colonjies have not been sewered 
so far. Action taken by Delhi Jal Board includes preparation of desilting and 
rehabilitation of sewage lines and augmentation of Sewage Treatment Plant 
(STP) from 482.4 MG D at present, to 710.4 MG D by 10th Five Year Plan. 
The Delhi Vidyut Board (now Delhi Power Supply Company) has stated 
that power requirements in Delhi has grown @7.8% in last three years in terms 
of maximum demand and energy requirement. Against a projected demand of 
3200 M.W. during July, 2002, there has been a shortfall in the availability from 
different sources. However, the transmission and distribution system has been 
augmented on continuous basis commensurate with the load growth in the 
concerned areas, Arrangements have also been made from time to time to ensure 
adequate power supply from various sources. 
To decongest Delhi, the Government had set up the National Capital Region 
Planning Board (NCRPB) through an Act of 1985. The Regional Plan 2001 for 
National Capital Region was notified in 1989, with the twin objectives of 
reducing population pressure by deflecting migration and achieving a balanced 
and harmonized development of the Region. 
The steps taken by NCR Planning Board to decongest Delhi include:— 
(i) Preparation of Regional Plan 2001 which is being implemented by the 
NCR States and the Central Ministries. 
(ii) Preparation of 4 functional Plans relating to Transportation, 
Telecommunications, Industry and Power. 
(iii) The preparation of the Sub-Regional Plan of Uttar Pradesh and 
Rajasthan sub-region. 
366 

[30 July, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
(iv) Extension of loan facilities to State Government/Agencies to create 
infrastructure so that pressure on Delhi is reduced.

368

(a) to (c) Under National Slum Development Programme (NSDP) every year 
funds in the form of Additional Central Assistance (ACA) are allocated by the 
Planning Commission, on the basis of slum population of the State/ Union 
Territory, for the development of urban slum. The funding is on the pattern of 
70% loan and 30% grant for non-special category States and 10% loan and

Planning Commission. However, the funds could not be allocated in view of the 
prescribed guidelines of NSDP and due to financial constraints.

SHRIMATI BIMBA RAIKAR (Karnataka): Madam, I rise to mention 
the enormous problems which arise on account of anti-environment activities, 
and the callous attitude of the Government in preventing them. We are all 
aware of the problem of water scarcity in the country. This problem has 
become an integral part of our life for years now; especially, the level of the 
underground water is going down and down. Before it gets exhausted, we 
should revive it; otherwise, the consequences might prove very grave. Severe 
deforestation has been taking place for decades resulting in environment 
imbalance, huge shortfall of rain, rise in temperature levels, etc. Unending 
usage of polythene, insufficient afforestation programmes,   ever-growing  
population,   industrial  waste  disposal  througn

Distress sale of paddy in Orissa 
MS. PRAMILA BOHIDAR (Orissa): Madam, distress sale of various 
products by farmers in many parts of the country this year has created havoc, 
and the farmers have been the worst sufferers. Since there have been no 
takers for paddy, particularly in parts of Baragarh, Sonepur and Sambalpur 
Districts of Orissa, which come under the Hirakud Command Area, the farmers 
are forced to sell their paddy at much below the Minimum Support Price fixed 
by the Union Government. Madam, Orissa's economy is primarily based on 
agriculture, and paddy is the major source of income for the farmers. The 
distress sale has broken the backbone of our farmers. The performance of the 
FCI, which is mainly responsible for procurement of foodgrains at the minimum 
support price, has been very discouraging. On the pretext of shortage of 
storage facility, etc., the FCI did not make timely procurement, as per the 
target fixed by the State Government. The decision of the Union Government 
to dispatch surplus paddy from other States to Orissa for storage purposes, 
has also aggravated the situation. 
Keeping in view the experience of the current year, I would urge upon 
the Ministry of Food and Consumer Affairs to initiate necessary measures, 
including the creation of additional storage facilities, to prevent such 
occurrences in the coming procurement season, or else, the farmers of Orissa 
will have no other way left but to commit suicide, as has been happening in 
States like Andhra Pradesh.

democratic polity like ours, rule of law is the basic requirement and, for that

Constitution had desired that the Supreme Court should also sit at places

SHRI DWIJENDRA NATH SHARMAH (Assam): Madam, I wish to 
draw the kind attention of the Government to the grave situation which has

international ramifications.

SHRIMATI VANGA GEETHA (Andhra Pradesh): Mr. Vice-Chairman,  
Sir, I thank you for giving me this opportunity to speak. Sir, I support the Indian 
Medicine Central Council (Amendment) Bill, 2002. The people are still having

Homoeopathy, Unani and Siddha. The medicines are not only cheap, but are 
within the reach of the common man also. The people believe that they can get 
a permanent cure with the Indian medicines, without having any side effects. 
These days, every patient is turning from English medicines to Indian 
medicines. In the Statement of Objects and Reasons, it is mentioned: 
"There are instances when colleges being permitted in the first year 
were denied permission in subsequent years. The procedure adopted 
for increasing and decreasing the seats has also been far from 
satisfactory. Seats are increased or decreased without proper 
evaluation. The Central Government is not in a position to take 
corrective steps as it has neither the power to intervene nor it can 
give any direction to the Central Council." 
Sir, since the Central Council has failed to live up to the expectations 
of the Government of India, this legislation is being enacted to empower the 
Government of India to intervene for improving the standard of Indian medical 
colleges and institutions. 
Sir, I have to make two or three suggestions in this regard. The 
power to sanction new colleges and courses should vest with the Central 
Council, and the Central Council should ensure the quality of education and 
the minimum standards of medical colleges.

deemed to be a recognised medical qualification for the purposes of this Act". 
Instead of this, you should have inserted a proviso or a penal provision, 
saying that those persons who were going to establish any medical institution 
without the permission of the Central Government, would be put behind bars; 
and there would be imprisonment for six or seven years. If that was done, only 
then the objectives would be fulfilled. Otherwise, you are going to penalise the 
poor student who comes forward to pursue his studies, believing what that 
institution or management says, and you are allowing these people to go scot-
free. It is not the ordinary people who open such institutions. Only those who 
have sufficient money, come forward to establish such institutions, and you 
are allowing them to go scot-free, with the money, and without any liability. In 
view of this, we do need a proviso and a penal provision here. 
There is another provision which is very astonishing. In clause 
13B(2), it is stated, "Where any medical institution opens a new or higher 
course of study or training including a post-graduate course of study or 
training without the previous permission of the Central Government in 
accordance with the provisions of section 13A, medical qualification granted to 
any student of such institution on the basis of such study or training shall not 
be deemed to be a recognised medical qualification for the purposes of this 
Act".  Again, here, you should have inserted a penal clause. 
Then, the last one, clause 13B(3), is very dangerous. It needs 
immediate intervention by the law-makers. It says, "Where any medical 
institution increases its admission capacity in any course of study or training 
without the previous permission of the Central Government in accordance with 
the provisions of section 13A, medical qualification granted to any student of 
such medical institution on the basis of the increase in its admission capacity 
shall not be deemed to be a recognised medical qualification for the purposes 
of this Act". Mr. Minister, I would like to draw your attention to this. Suppose 
you fix a quota of 100 seats per year for  a particular institution. They take Rs. 
10-15 lakhs per seat. There is a rush of students and the poor students do not 
know what the total capacity of that institution is. The management does not 
disclose how many seats had already been filled. Suppose they take 25 
students more. What will happen is that, according to this provision, the 
medical degrees given to the last 25 students will not be recognised.   Whose 
fault will it be?   In such a case, 
444

there should be a provision that the day those 100 seats are filled, the 
management should notify it on the notice board, giving the details of all the 
100 seats, including the names of students, and so on. Otherwise, I feel there 
would be some sort of encouragement for these people because of the Act 
itself, because you are putting the burden on the student and not on the 
management. The student who has paid the donation, who has studied for 
three or four years, would have to suffer without a degree for his whole life. 
This is the flaw in the Act. I would request the hon. Minister to insert a clause 
here, shifting the burden on the institution or the management that is involved 
in opening the institution, that they should not admit more number of students 
that what is allotted to them. 
With these words, I welcome this Bill.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): Sir, when I moved this Bill, last Friday, 
our late Vice-President and the hon. Chairman of this House, Shri Krishan 
Kant, was in the Chair. He heard me on that day, when I moved the Bill. and 
then, some of the Members had spoken on that day. Then he adjourned the 
House for lunch. I recall that today. And I express my condolences on his sad 
demise. His role as a Parliamentarian, and, above all, as a statesman, will 
inspire us. the people of younger generation. 
Sir, I thank the Members who have spoken on this Bill. Some 
common points were made by hon. Members, including on our own system, 
the Indian system of healthcare delivery, and the Budgetary support being 
given to it. Sir, no doubt, as hon. Member, Shri Viduthalai Virumbi, has put it, 
together with' the private sector, our country is spending only 5.2% of the 
GDP, whereas the developed countries are spending between 10% and 12%; 
and some countries are even spending 15%. Out of this 5.2% of the GDP, 
honestly, I can share with the hon. Members, about only one per cent is spent 
from the Government side. 
Sir, Shri Rahman Khan and others had expressed their deep 
concern over the Budgetary support, and the spending mode of the 
Government towards health care, including on the Indian systems of 
medicine. Sir, because of the financial constraint, not only in the health sector, 
but in all other Ministries we are facing difficulties. At the same time, we are 
trying to give safe and efficacious medicines, and good standard of medical 
education throughout the country. 
Sir, the intention of this legislation is--it is needless to submit before 
the House--to bring about parity with the allopathic system. We are having the 
Indian Medical Council Act for the allopathic system, whether it is MBBS or MD 
or any other course. The other day, some of the hon. Members said that 
whenever a law is legislated in the House, it did not seem to be foolproof. We 
enacted the Dowry (Prohibition) Act; that doesn't mean that dowry deaths 
have been stopped. We have enacted the PCR Act; it doesn't mean that 
untouchability has gone out of this country. 
Similarly, if at all some deficiencies are there, the intention of the 
Government in bringing in this piece of legislation is to plug the loopholes that 
are in the existing law. Sir, it is nothing but a law which gives a full picture, 
which gives parity with the allopathic system of medical education, with 
symmetrical and identical provisions.

Sir, when we talk of the background of the Indian systems of 
medicine, it is not that it is available only in Tamil Nadu. Someone was saying 
that Siddha could be considered as prevalent only in Tamil Nadu. Some 
people may say that ayurveda belongs only to Gujarat or Kerala. The global 
system is like this. It is not India only but many other countries including UK, 
USA, Austria, Australia, and other countries are turning to their own traditional 
system of medicine. I can share a few words with the House in this regard. Sir, 
according to a report prepared by Mc Alpine Thorpe and Warrier Limited, the 
global herbal market is estimated to be worth of Rs.51,000 crores. Out of this, 
the Indian export is only worth Rs.480 crores which is 0.5 per cent of the total 
export market while the share of China's exports is 35.3 per cent of the total 
market. Coming to the people's modus operandi of those who are turning to 
traditional system of medicine when it is compared to India, people abroad are 
quickly and rapidly changing their attitude and lifestyle towards the traditional 
system of medicine. In Australia 48 per cent of the people have turned to their 
own system of medicine than to the allopathic system. They say their 
traditional system of medicine is preventive in nature whereas the allopathic 
system is curative in nature. In USA this percentage is 42 per cent and in 
France- this percentage is almost 75 per cent. In UK this is 90 per cent. This 
percentage of population has used this traditional system of medicine system 
at least, once. So, the global scenario has changed. As far as seminars are 
concerned, India is continuously interacting with other countries. There have 
been many seminars and fairs in this regard. Many MoUs have been signed 
between India and other countries. A delegation from India visited Russia to 
sign an MoU in Ayurveda and Unani. A delegation also visited Malaysia to 
know the usage of their traditional system of medicines. In turn, Malaysia has 
expressed its willingness to take the Indian systems of medicine including 
Ayurveda. I led a delegation to South Africa. They are looking at our system of 
medicine and our process of marketing. They are ready to adopt a reciprocal 
attitude towards India. A delegation from India went to UK, South Africa and 
Moscow. The global scenario has changed in such a manner that not only the 
allopathic system of medicine but the Indian systems of medicine also are 
spreading all over the world. They want our traditional system. This global 
spenario is not only in tbe field of herbal products for treatment but this 
scepario is there in the case of other medicines, capsules, etc. There-is a 
homogenous and global scene. Sir, after' having seen and known this global 
scenario, our intention is that there should be a uniform and homogenous 
system of 
448 

[30 July, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
education. There should not be ANY disparities among the States. Suppose, 
one State gives permission to start a college for a three-year degree course in 
Ayurveda, and some other State, say, Kerala, gives the same degree in two 
years, then, that aspect can be governed. There is a symmetrical and identical 
system as it is in the case of allopathic system. That is why we have made this 
provision in this piece of legislation. I can say to that extent in this regard. 
Now, I would like to pinpoint some of the allegations that have been made by 
one of the hon. Members. I think he is a learned lawyer. He said that clause 13 
(a) says that if the Government is keeping mum for one year after getting the 
proposal from a particular institution, it should be deemed as recognised. The 
letter and spirit of the law says - if he ^ees the parent Act and not the 
amending Bill, that all the formalities have been fulfilled -- as contemplated by 
law, which means, all the formalities enumerated in the parent Act have been 
duly complied with by the college and then application comes for revision to 
the Ministry or the Council. I can share with the hon. Members that the Indian 
Medical Council is in a mess. Its Chairman has been removed by the court and 
an administrator has been appointed by the court itself. There is a gulf 
between the Executive Members and the Chairman. Because of this gulf, the 
Council is not doing well. I can tell the hon. House that because of this many 
colleges are being prevented from getting recognition. So, in such 
circumstances, a college should not be deprived of any approval. It is because 
of that this clause has been incorporated. There is no other reason behind in 
incorporating this clause. If the proposal is in order, definitely the Council will 
give its approval. Suppose, there is any default on the part of the Government, 
or, if there is any default on the part of the Council due to internal differences, 
the institution, which has submitted its application for opening of a college, 
should not be deprived of getting approval. It is with this intention that this 
clause has been incorporated to regulate the speedy disposal of applications. 
It is not a weapon against the colleges, but it is aimed at encouraging colleges 
to start the academic year at appropriate time with their syllabus and 
curriculum. 
With regard to the point raised by  Shri Viduthalai Virumbi and Smt. 
Indira about the National Institute of Siddha, I would like to submit that all 
other systems of medicine are having their own national institutes. In the same 
way, Siddha is also having its own institute. As Mr. Virumbi has rightly 
mentioned, when Dr. M. Karunanidhi was the Chief Minister of Tamil Nadu, he 
was kind enough to allot a piece of land, free of cost, for this purpose.   Last 
year, the Central Government had sanctioned, in principle, an 
449 

RAJYA SABHA [30 July, 2002] 
amount of Rs. 47 crores for the National Institute of Siddha. I am confident 
that within two years the construction would be over. The construction has 
been entrusted to a public sector undertaking. I hope that within two to three 
years, it would be completed and by that time the institute will become 
operational. 
If there is any apprehension in the minds of the hon. Members 
pertaining to their own State or any individual case, it would be my endeavour 
to clarify the same. 
With these words, I conclude my speech. 
So, Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, t request the House, once again, to pass 
this legislation.  Thank you.
